title: Practice Set PMSI4 — Manual Salting and Other Interventions
description: Mid recognition track: choose between manual salting and AQE skew handling. Compute correct salt factors. Recognize the rand()-based salt that disappears after AQE re-execution — the same root cause from PJSI4.2 expressed as a memory cascade.

datasets.description: Schema reference (sample rows). Mid memory & skew scenarios reference NordGrid at mid production scale (12M meters across 12 regions, 24× the junior dataset).
Substations reference (~200 rows at mid scale). Anchors broadcast-eligibility scenarios.

tasks.title: Salting Factor Calculation — Two Approaches Compared

description.context: Two NordGrid mid-level engineers solve the same skew problem differently. The pipeline aggregates 12M meter rows by customer_type, where customer_type follows the 60/25/12/3 NordGrid distribution. Both engineers add salting to spread the skewed RESIDENTIAL key. Engineer A picks salt factor 10. Engineer B computes the salt factor based on the data distribution.
description.task: Which salt factor is correct, and what is the cost trade-off?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Key Distribution: RESIDENTIAL 60%, COMMERCIAL 25%, INDUSTRIAL 12%, PROSUMER 3%

Shuffle Partitions: 200

Rows Per Task Target: ~60K rows (12M / 200)

evidence.label: Engineer A — salt factor 10
evidence.content:
# Append a 0-9 salt suffix
salted = meters.withColumn(
    'customer_type_salted',
    concat(col('customer_type'), lit('_'),
           (f_abs(hash(col('meter_id'))) % 10).cast('int')))

partial = salted.groupBy('customer_type_salted').agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('p'))
result = (partial.withColumn('customer_type', split('customer_type_salted', '_')[0])
                 .groupBy('customer_type').agg(sum('p').alias('total')))

evidence.label: Engineer B — salt factor based on dominance
evidence.content:
# Salt factor = dominant_share / minor_share = 60% / 0.5% ≈ 120
salted = meters.withColumn(
    'customer_type_salted',
    concat(col('customer_type'), lit('_'),
           (f_abs(hash(col('meter_id'))) % 120).cast('int')))

partial = salted.groupBy('customer_type_salted').agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('p'))
result = (partial.withColumn('customer_type', split('customer_type_salted', '_')[0])
                 .groupBy('customer_type').agg(sum('p').alias('total')))

fields.label: Which salt factor is correct, and what is the cost trade-off?
options: A (factor 10) is correct — 10 is the canonical default. Salt factor 120 over-engineers and produces 12× more output rows in partial aggregation, slowing post-aggregation by 12×.
Both equivalent in correctness; salt factor only affects parallelism. A produces 4×10=40 partial buckets, B produces 4×120=480; pick A as cheaper at this scale and same final result.
B (factor 120) is correct. RESIDENTIAL = 60% × 12M = 7.2M rows in ONE bucket. Factor 10 → 720K per bucket, still 12× target. Factor 120 → 60K per bucket, matching target.

Neither — salt factor must be a power of 2 (8, 16, 32, 64, 128) for Spark's hash to distribute evenly. Both 10 and 120 produce hash collisions. Correct factor: 128 (closest power of 2 to B's calculation).
fields.correctAnswer: B (factor 120) is correct. RESIDENTIAL = 60% × 12M = 7.2M rows in ONE bucket. Factor 10 → 720K per bucket, still 12× target. Factor 120 → 60K per bucket, matching target.
fields.rationale: Salting works by splitting one skewed key into N synthetic keys.The right N depends on the data.2M rows; target per task = 60K.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Reverses cost-benefit.Over-salting cost is logarithmic; under-salting leaves linear skew cost.
Option B: Treats salt as parallelism only.

tasks.psReference: PSI3 lesson 5 (Resolving Skew with Salting), PSI3 lesson 5b (Salt Factor Calculation).

tasks.title: The Salt That Disappeared After AQE

description.context: A NordGrid mid-level engineer added hand-rolled salting to their join eight months ago to handle customer_type skew. The pipeline worked correctly when AQE was disabled. After Platform enabled AQE by default last month, the same pipeline started producing rows with NULL on the salted_dim columns — not consistently, but enough to fail downstream validation. The cascade of failed retries triggers executor OOMs that the engineer initially misdiagnoses as memory pressure. Cross-references PJSI4.2 (joins angle).
description.task: What is the bug, why do executor OOMs appear, and why does raising --executor-memory not fix them?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Salt Factor: 10

Aqe State: enabled cluster-default since last month

Primary Failure: intermittent NULLs in salted_dim columns post-join

Secondary Failure: executor OOMs on stage retries; raising --executor-memory does not help

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, expr, lit, concat

# Salt the meters side: append random 0-9 suffix
salted_meters = meters.withColumn(
    'customer_type_salted',
    concat(col('customer_type'), lit('_'),
           (expr('rand() * 10').cast('int'))))

# Replicate the dim side: 10 rows per customer_type
salted_dim = (customer_type_dim
    .crossJoin(spark.range(10).withColumnRenamed('id', 'salt'))
    .withColumn('customer_type_salted',
        concat(col('customer_type'), lit('_'), col('salt').cast('int'))))

# Join on the salted key
result = salted_meters.join(salted_dim, on='customer_type_salted', how='left')

fields.label: What is the bug, why do executor OOMs appear, and why does raising --executor-memory not fix them?
options: Shuffle buffer running out during the salt-driven repartition; --executor-memory should help but spark.shuffle.memoryFraction is set too low to actually use the additional heap. Fix: raise spark.shuffle.memoryFraction.

rand() is non-deterministic. AQE re-evaluation may run salting with new values. salted_meters and salted_dim then mismatch. Joins miss → retries → tasks pile on survivors → OOMs. Fix: pmod(crc32(meter_id), 10).

The crossJoin produces 10× rows on the dim side; inflation forces sort-merge instead of broadcast, sort-merge spills, spill triggers OOMs. Fix: broadcast the dim side explicitly with broadcast() hint.

AQE's coalesce-shuffle-partitions reduced the partition count below 10, mapping multiple salt values to the same partition; the salt's pre-condition is invalidated. Fix: disable AQE for this stage with /*+ NO_AQE */.
fields.correctAnswer: rand() is non-deterministic. AQE re-evaluation may run salting with new values. salted_meters and salted_dim then mismatch. Joins miss → retries → tasks pile on survivors → OOMs. Fix: pmod(crc32(meter_id), 10).
fields.distractorRationale:
6+.
Option C: Confuses crossJoin row inflation (real concern) with the cause of NULLs (rand() non-determinism).

tasks.psReference: PSI3 lesson 5 (Salting), PSI3 lesson 6 (AQE limitations), PSI8 lesson 3 (OOM Diagnosis — root cause vs cascade). Cross-reference: PJSI4.2 covers the same root cause from the join-correctness angle.
